planting.note: Start indoors, surface-sowing the fine seed since it needs light to germinate; transplant after frost danger passes into a spot with room for the tall, airy, branching habit to develop fully.

directions: Start seed indoors, pressing it lightly into the surface of the mix without covering, and transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade once frost danger has passed. This tall, gracefully branching flowering tobacco produces hundreds of small, star-shaped blooms that open white or pale pink and darken through rose to deep magenta as they age, giving each plant a cloud of multiple colors at once — the trait behind both its common name and species epithet. Unlike the more compact bedding nicotianas, it blooms freely in daylight rather than mainly at dusk, making it a favorite for cutting gardens and airy, see-through plantings toward the back of a border. It self-sows readily in mild climates and, though grown as an annual, can persist as a short-lived perennial in zone 9 and warmer.

planting.note: Direct sow after the danger of hard frost has passed, since the taprooted seedlings resent transplanting; thin to final spacing once seedlings have a couple of true leaves.

directions: Direct sow into well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, since the deep taproot makes this Mediterranean annual a poor candidate for transplanting from cell packs. Malope produces large, satiny, mallow-like flowers in shades of magenta, pink, or white, each backed by three enlarged leafy bracts that continue to enlarge and remain attractive as the seed pod matures, giving the plant a long season of interest beyond the bloom itself. Sturdy, upright, and free-flowering over a long summer season, it makes an easy, old-fashioned cottage garden and cutting-garden annual that needs little more than deadheading to keep producing new flowers. Once established it tolerates heat and some drought well, and it self-sows modestly where the soil is left undisturbed.
